ambiguous

/am-BIG-yoo-us/ — stress on BIG · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is ambiguous can be understood in more than one way, so its exact meaning stays unclear.

The treasure map's final clue was ambiguous: 'below the old stone' could mean a dozen places.

Example

The job posting's description was ambiguous, stating that the role required 'significant experience' without defining whether that meant 5 years or 15 years.

Ambi (both, two ways) + gere (to wander/go) + -ous (full of) = full of both-ways-ness. An ambiguous meaning wanders in two directions at once—it can be read or understood as more than one thing. The job description could mean experienced or it could mean less experienced, depending on how you interpret 'significant.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

vague: A vague answer is thin on detail — it gives too little information to pin anything down. An ambiguous answer is often rich in detail; the trouble is that its words support two or more definite readings. Vague starves you of meaning, while ambiguous hands you several meanings at once.

equivocal: Equivocal describes language made two-sided on purpose, usually so a speaker can dodge blame later — a politician's equivocal promise. Ambiguous is neutral about intent: a map clue or a rule can be ambiguous by accident. If the double meaning looks intentional, call it equivocal; ambiguous only reports that two readings exist.

murky: A murky situation is hard to see into, the way muddy water hides what lies beneath — facts are missing or tangled together. Ambiguous is more precise: everything is in plain view, but the wording supports more than one reading. Murky means you cannot make out the meaning; ambiguous means you make out two.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unambiguous: having exactly one clear meaning

clear: easy to understand; leaving no confusion

Where it sits · how many different meanings it allows

fuzzy → unclear → confusing → ambiguous

fuzzy vs. ambiguous: A fuzzy answer just lacks sharp detail, but an ambiguous answer could mean two opposite things.

unclear vs. ambiguous: An unclear direction slows you down; an ambiguous direction can send you the wrong way entirely.

confusing vs. ambiguous: A confusing announcement scrambles its message until no reading emerges, but an ambiguous announcement reads smoothly and still supports two rival meanings.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ambigu: to wander both ways — from Latin ambigere; not a standalone English word (Latin (ambigere))

Suffix — -ous: full of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together: The base ambigu- is not a standalone English word; it comes from Latin ambigere, 'to wander both ways.' Add -ous ('full of') and ambiguous means 'full of both-ways-ness' — a message that wanders between two possible meanings.

Use the root in a new word: ambiguity: The lawyer removed every ambiguity from the contract so no one could misread its terms.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Reach for ambiguous when something has two or more legitimate meanings or interpretations. An ambiguous statement, an ambiguous ending, an ambiguous rule—the word flags that more than one reading is possible. It's useful in describing intentional wordplay and unintentional confusion alike.
